title: How would you design the on-call rotation and paging for this system?
summary: Tests whether you think about on-call as a design input — who gets paged for what, how alerts map to ownership — rather than an afterthought bolted on post-launch.

slides.markdown:
On-call design shows up as a system-design question because who gets paged for what is an architectural decision, not an operational afterthought — it depends directly on how the system is decomposed into services and who owns each one.

The interviewer wants to see you treat paging and rotation as a design input: alerts routed to the team that actually owns the failing component, with a clear, time-boxed escalation path, rather than a vague "someone would get paged."

Ask how many teams or services are involved — a single-team service has a simple answer; a system spanning several teams needs a real routing design, not just "the on-call engineer."

Ask whether ownership maps cleanly to alerting already, or whether that mapping itself needs to be designed. In many real systems, alerts were bolted on as services were built, with no one having deliberately decided which team should be paged for which failure — that gap is often the actual problem being tested here.

Route alerts to the team that owns the failing component, with a clear escalation path if the page goes unacknowledged. Ownership-based routing is the core design decision — everything else (rotation size, escalation timers) builds on top of getting this mapping right.

The skeleton is deceptively simple to state and genuinely hard to execute at scale, because ownership boundaries shift as a system evolves and alerts need to be kept in sync with who actually owns what. For the broader alerting design this plugs into, see [alerting and on-call design](alerting-and-on-call-design).

A paging policy with a primary and secondary rotation, plus a 15-minute escalation timer: if the primary hasn't acknowledged the page within 15 minutes, it escalates to the secondary; if that also goes unacknowledged, it escalates further to the team lead.

Each step in that chain has a concrete, named person or role and a specific time limit — nothing in the policy depends on someone remembering to escalate manually or guessing how long is "too long" to wait for an acknowledgment.

A checkout-service alert firing pages the checkout team directly, rather than a generic "backend on-call," because the alert was defined with clear component ownership from the start. That cuts the average time-to-first-response from 12 minutes — the time a generic on-call engineer spent figuring out which team actually owned the failing component — down to under 2 minutes.

The 10-minute difference here is entirely attributable to the routing design, not to the responders being faster once paged — the generic on-call engineer in the old setup wasn't slower at fixing things, they just spent most of that 12 minutes figuring out who to hand it to.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: sizing the rotation itself
slides.markdown:
A single-person rotation burns out fast and has zero coverage for illness or vacation — the moment that person is unavailable, there's no on-call at all. Most teams run a rotation of at least 4-6 engineers to keep any one person's on-call burden to roughly one week a month or less.

This isn't an arbitrary number — it's derived from a sustainability target: a rotation smaller than that means each person is on-call disproportionately often, which is exactly the setup that leads to burnout and eventually attrition off the rotation entirely, making the problem worse over time.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
Narrower, per-team ownership of alerts gets the right person paged faster but requires more alert-routing setup and can create gaps at team boundaries.

| Approach | Response speed | Setup cost |
|---|---|---|
| Per-team, ownership-based routing | Fast — the right team is paged directly | Higher — every alert needs explicit ownership mapping, kept current |
| Single catch-all on-call | Slow — most pages route to someone who then has to find the real owner | Lower — one rotation to maintain |

A single catch-all is simpler to set up but routes almost every page to someone who then has to figure out who actually owns the problem — the checkout scenario's 12-minute-to-2-minute gap is exactly this trade-off playing out in practice.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: an alert fires for a shared dependency three teams depend on
slides.markdown:
Page the team that owns the shared dependency itself — not all three consuming teams — with the affected teams **notified**, not paged, so they have visibility without diluting responsibility for the actual fix.

Paging all three dependent teams for the same underlying issue creates confused, uncoordinated response (echoing the three-engineers-collide failure mode from incident response) without adding any real fixing power, since none of the three teams own the component that's actually broken.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: is your on-call load sustainable?
slides.markdown:
Track pages-per-shift and off-hours pages per person over time, not just whether the rotation is technically staffed. A sustained rise in either — especially in low-value, non-actionable pages — is the leading indicator to fix before you lose the engineer, not after they've already burned out or left the rotation.

This metric should feed back into both alert quality (are pages actually actionable?) and rotation size (is the load spread across enough people?) — sustainability isn't a single fix, it's an ongoing measurement that catches decay in either dimension before it becomes a resignation.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: routing everything to one catch-all on-call
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We have one on-call rotation for the whole backend team — that's simpler than mapping every alert to a specific owner."

**Why it's wrong:** it guarantees slow response, since whoever's paged has to first figure out which component actually failed and who owns it before they can even start fixing anything — exactly the 12-minute gap in the checkout scenario in this topic. Over time, it also concentrates burnout on whoever's most senior or most willing to dig into unfamiliar systems under pressure.

**Correct model:** invest in ownership-based routing up front, even though it costs more setup — the response-time and sustainability gains compound over every incident that follows, while the setup cost is paid once.

Route alerts to the team that owns the failing component, with a time-boxed escalation path (primary, then secondary, then a lead) if a page goes unacknowledged. Size the rotation to at least 4-6 engineers so no one person carries a disproportionate on-call burden.

For a shared dependency, page its owning team and notify the dependents, rather than paging everyone. Track pages-per-shift over time as the leading indicator of sustainability, and invest in ownership-based routing up front — a single catch-all rotation is simpler to build but guarantees slower response and concentrated burnout.
